title: One soul
hook: He created you from a single soul and made its mate, so respect the wombs that bore you (4:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Al 'Imran: standing, sitting, lying down, and Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Your line was not in vain. Did you look at the sky? Day three hundred seventy-six, and a new surah.

At a great many Muslim weddings, before the vows, someone stands and gives a short sermon that the Prophet ﷺ used to open important speeches. It quotes three verses. One of them is the first verse of the fourth surah, an-Nisa, the Women. So as two families are being joined, the room hears a verse about where all families came from. Today, that verse, and the opening of a surah that will spend a long time on family, inheritance and fairness.
screen: `A SERMON BEFORE THE VOWS.` → `AN-NISA, THE WOMEN.` → `WHERE ALL FAMILIES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Surah 4 opens by speaking to everyone: O mankind. Then, in Pickthall's words, be careful of your duty to your Lord "Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate." And from those two, the verse says, He spread abroad many men and women. One soul. Nafs wahida. Before any nation, tribe, language or family name, there's a single origin. Every person you'll meet today is, in the verse's picture, a relative. Then comes a phrase that's easy to pass over: be mindful of God, by whom you ask things of one another, and of the arham. Arham means wombs, and by extension it means kinship, the ties of family. And here's the detail. Rahim, womb, comes from the same root as rahma, mercy, and ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes the link explicit: the word for womb is taken from the name ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps its ties, God keeps ties with them. So the surah of the Women begins by placing mothers, wombs and family ties right next to God's own mercy. That's why it fits a wedding. Two families joining are reminded they were already one, and reminded what they owe each other. In the coming days, an-Nisa will get very specific: orphans, inheritance shares, kindness in marriage, neighbors near and far. It all grows out of this first verse. One soul, many people, ties of mercy between them.
screen: `O MANKIND: SPOKEN TO EVERYONE` · `NAFS WAHIDA: ONE SOUL` · `ARHAM: WOMBS, AND KINSHIP` · `RAHIM AND RAHMA: ONE ROOT` · then, large: `FROM A SINGLE SOUL.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of your mother, or whoever carried and raised you. If she's living and you can, plan to call her today. If she has died, or if that relationship is hard, you can simply hold her in mind for a moment, or think of another woman who mothered you. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for her. Then widen the circle: picture the people around you today, strangers included, and remember the verse's claim: from one soul. The bell holds the time.
One soul. Nafs wahida: all people from a single soul and its mate, the opening of an-Nisa, 4:1. Today's word.
Your line: from one soul. Today, call your mother or pray for her, and treat one stranger as the relative the verse says they are. Day three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Muslims hear 4:1 in the khutbat al-hajah, the Prophet's opening sermon recited at many weddings and Friday sermons, and the verse is a basis for keeping ties of kinship, silat al-rahim, a duty stressed throughout Islamic teaching.

pairs: mercy, from the same root as womb

myth: womb and mercy share a root in Arabic
rahim and rahma, r-h-m, and a hadith in Bukhari links the womb to the name ar-Rahman.
this verse is often heard at weddings
it is one of the three verses in the khutbat al-hajah, recited before many marriages.

fork.setup: you're at a Muslim wedding. before the vows, a short sermon quotes three verses. one of them is about what?
options: all people created from a single soul.
the story of a famous couple.
fork.reveal: 4:1: created from a single soul, and mindful of the ties of the womb. two families are reminded they were already one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse about Adam and Eve.
what it means: all people come from one soul, so every person is kin, and family ties are tied to God's mercy.
what a scholar hears: arham read both as wombs and kinship; the r-h-m root shared with ar-Rahman; and the verse's place in the khutbat al-hajah.
